config.title: Role-Based Route Protection

intro.title: Role-Based Route Protection
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple React application that protects certain routes based on a user's role. You will learn how to conditionally render components and restrict navigation using role-based logic. The core concepts involve React Router for navigation and TypeScript for type-safe user roles. You'll create a basic user authentication simulation and implement a protected route component. By the end, you'll understand how to control access to different parts of your app based on user permissions.
intro.usecase: Role-based route protection is essential in applications where different users have different levels of access, such as enterprise dashboards, admin panels, or SaaS platforms. For example, in a project management tool, an admin might see all project settings and user management pages, while a regular team member only sees task boards and reports. This pattern ensures security and a tailored user experience by restricting UI components like navigation menus, data tables, or configuration forms based on user roles, preventing unauthorized access to sensitive features.

objectives: Implement a role-based authentication context to manage user roles globally
Construct protected route components that conditionally render based on user roles
Configure route definitions with role requirements using TypeScript interfaces
Integrate role checks within navigation components to control access
Apply conditional rendering logic to display appropriate UI for different user roles
Initialize and update role state within React components using hooks
Manipulate routing behavior programmatically based on authentication status

steps.instruction: Create a TypeScript type alias named 'UserRole' that defines three possible string literal values: 'admin', 'user', and 'guest'.
steps.hint: Use the 'type' keyword followed by the type name and an equals sign. Then define the union of string literals using the pipe (|) operator.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: defining a type for status values
type Status = 'pending' | 'success' | 'error';

successCriteria: The UserRole type is defined with the three string literal values 'admin', 'user', and 'guest' using TypeScript union syntax.

steps.title: Create authentication context
steps.instruction: Create a React context named AuthContext using createContext. Provide a default value of null and explicitly type it to allow a user object with role property of type UserRole or null.
steps.hint: Use createContext to create a context. The type should be an object with role: UserRole or null. Set the initial value to null.
steps.analogousExample:
// Creating a typed context
const ThemeContext = createContext<'light' | 'dark' | null>(null);
steps.expectedOutcome: A typed AuthContext is created with proper TypeScript annotations and a default value of null.
successCriteria: AuthContext is created using createContext with type { role: UserRole } | null and default value null.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You created a context, but check the type annotation or default value.
steps.feedbackWrong: The AuthContext is missing or incorrectly typed. Ensure it uses createContext with the correct type.

steps.title: Create AuthProvider component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named AuthProvider that takes children as props and returns a wrapper element.
steps.hint: Define a component that accepts props and returns JSX. You'll need to wrap children in a provider element later.
steps.expectedOutcome: A functional component named AuthProvider is defined with props and a return statement.
successCriteria: AuthProvider component is created as a functional component that accepts children props and returns JSX.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created the AuthProvider component structure.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started the component, but make sure it accepts children props and returns JSX.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component isn't defined correctly. Create a functional component named AuthProvider that takes children and returns JSX.

steps.title: Create useAuth custom hook
steps.instruction: Create a custom hook named 'useAuth' that returns the authentication context value. The hook should throw an error if used outside of AuthProvider.
steps.hint: Use the useContext hook to access the authentication context. Check if the context value is undefined to determine if it's being used outside the provider.
steps.expectedOutcome: A custom hook named 'useAuth' is created that provides access to the authentication context with proper error handling.
successCriteria: The useAuth hook is defined, uses useContext to access the authentication context, includes error handling for usage outside the provider, and returns the context value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created a custom hook, but it might be missing error handling or proper context access. Make sure to use useContext and check if the context value is undefined.
steps.feedbackWrong: The useAuth hook isn't properly implemented. Remember to create a function named 'useAuth' that uses useContext to access the authentication context and includes error handling.

steps.title: Create ProtectedRoute component with role checking
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named ProtectedRoute that takes props: allowedRoles (array of UserRole) and children (ReactNode). Use the useAuth hook to get the current user role and conditionally render children only if the user's role is included in allowedRoles.
steps.hint: Define the component with proper TypeScript props interface. Inside, call useAuth() to get userRole, then check if userRole exists and is in allowedRoles. Return children if allowed, otherwise null or a fallback message.
steps.expectedOutcome: A ProtectedRoute component is defined that uses useAuth to check the user's role against allowedRoles and conditionally renders its children.
successCriteria: It accepts allowedRoles and children props with correct types
It uses useAuth to get userRole
It conditionally renders children based on role check
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure the component uses useAuth and checks if userRole is in allowedRoles before rendering children.
steps.feedbackWrong: The ProtectedRoute component is missing or incorrect. Ensure it's a functional component that takes allowedRoles and children props, uses useAuth, and conditionally renders based on role.

steps.title: Implement role-based redirect logic
steps.instruction: Inside the ProtectedRoute component, add logic that redirects unauthorized users to a login page when they lack the required role. Use the useAuth hook to get the current user and check if their role matches the required role prop.
steps.hint: You can use conditional rendering with a ternary operator. If the user's role doesn't match the required role, return a redirect component (like a Navigate component from react-router-dom) to '/login'.
steps.expectedOutcome: The ProtectedRoute component will now redirect users who don't have the required role to the login page, while allowing authorized users to see the protected content.
successCriteria: ProtectedRoute component contains logic that checks the user's role against requiredRole and redirects to '/login' when they don't match
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using the useAuth hook to get the current user and comparing their role with the requiredRole prop. Also ensure you're returning a redirect when the roles don't match.
steps.feedbackWrong: The redirect logic isn't implemented correctly. Remember to use the useAuth hook to access the current user, check if their role matches the requiredRole prop, and return a redirect to '/login' when they don't match.

steps.expectedOutcome: Each login button will trigger authentication with the appropriate role when clicked.
successCriteria: All three buttons have onClick handlers that call the login function with 'admin', 'user', and 'guest' roles respectively.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
